newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: BEST ON GROUND-ANDREW BARTRAM'S AUSSIE RULES COLUMN.
newsitem.headline: BEST ON GROUND-ANDREW BARTRAM'S AUSSIE RULES COLUMN.

text.p: By Andrew Bartram*
IT'S A LOG-JAM AT THE TOP.
Losses for three of the top five teams on the weekend changed the complexion of the AFL ladder and ensured that the race for the 1997 premiership will go right to the wire.
Such is the congestion at the top that no team in the eight at the beginning of round 19 finished the weekend in the same position on the ladder.

The big movers upwards were Adelaide (second to first) after defeating Port Adelaide in the local derby, St Kilda (fourth to second) by doing the improbable and beating the Swans in Sydney, North Melbourne (sixth to fifth) and West Coast (seventh to sixth).
The latter pair moved to within a few percentage points of a top four berth and a home final.
Geelong dropped from first to third after a inexplicable loss to Essendon, Sydney from third to fourth and Brisbane from fifth to eighth after the Kangaroos exposed it as a grand final pretender.
With three rounds to play before the finals, it looks certain that the grand finalists will come from the current top six but who they will be is mystery, for each team has legitimate claims.

Adelaide, an under-achiever since entering the competition in 1991, is finally doing justice to its talented list. St Kilda, for so long a laughing stock and perennial whipping boy, is combining on-ball class with forward potency.

Geelong, a four-time grand final loser since 1989 has a sense of destiny and stability about it. Sydney, runner-up last year, is seeking atonement. North Melbourne is looking to defy the odds and recent history by being the first team in the 1990s to win back-to-back flags.
West Coast, premiers twice this decade, is building an ominous challenge with a blend of experience and youth.

Western Bulldogs, Brisbane, Port Adelaide and Fremantle will be vying for seventh and eighth spots but will merely be making up the numbers unless Adelaide finishes on top and Port Adelaide eighth, which should make for an interesting final at Football Park.
THE VARIABLES
As always, injuries and suspension will play a major role in a team's fortunes.

North Melbourne's premiership chances were dealt a potentially crushing blow on Friday night when star ruckman Corey McKernan suffered a serious leg injury which, at best, will sideline him until mid-way through the finals series.

In addition to a serious knee injury to midfielder Grant Tanner, Geelong has an anxious wait while umpires scrutinise footage of an incident involving captain Barry Stoneham in which Essendon's Michael Symons suffered a broken jaw.
At this stage, the remaining contenders are relatively injury and suspension free.
GIESCHEN SETS THE STANDARD.
He may be the new kid on the block but caretaker Richmond coach Jeff Gieschen has set a standard which others, most notably Essendon coach Kevin Sheedy, are following.

Against Western Bulldogs, in his first game as coach following the sacking of Robert Walls five days earlier, Gieschen addressed his three-quarter-time huddle near the boundary in front of the Tiger faithful to "milk the atmosphere" as he put it.
One player later noted that the players couldn't hear a word Gieschen said, such was the fervour from the terraces, but the Tigers were inspired enough to record a morale-boosting win.

Presumably, Gieschen intended using the same tactic during Saturday night's game against Fremantle in Perth but could not find enough Richmond supporters in the crowd to rouse his team which went on to lose the low scoring game by 42 points.
Kevin Sheedy followed Gieschen's lead when his lowly Bombers trailed Geelong by two points at three-quarter time in Sunday's clash at the MCG.

Sheedy spoke to his huddle in front of the Bomber faithful in the Great Southern Stand and the players responded with a stirring last quarter performance to edge out the Cats by five points and move from 15th to 14th on the ladder.
*Andrew Bartram will be writing a regular AFL column for Reuters. Any feedback to michael.stapleton@reuters.com
